candidates.source_summary: Northampton beat Rochdale 3-2 in a thrilling game at Sixfields.
candidates.source_body_excerpt:
Northampton beat Rochdale 3-2 in a thrilling game at Sixfields.

Both teams had the lead at different stages of a topsy-turvy encounter but Lee Evans' 74th-minute penalty ensured the home side claimed all three points.

Rochdale goalkeeper Sam Waller denied Matty Warhurst early on before Northampton took a deserved lead on 11 minutes when Owen Dale latched onto James Maxwell's ball down the left wing, cut inside and drilled into the bottom corner.

Waller was a busy man throughout the first half as his reflexes denied Joe O'Brien-Whitmarsh before he also thwarted Dale and Joe Wormleighton.

Rochdale were second best up until the break but they were a different team in the second half and scored twice in as many minutes to turn things around.

Ed Francis' shot from 25 yards squirmed through Zach Jeacock before Cian Hayes slid home at the back post from Glenn Middleton's cross.

Northampton fought back impressively though, Elliott List tucking away Warhurst's cutback midway through the second half, before Evans won it from 12 yards with 16 minutes to go after a penalty was given for handball.

candidates.source_summary: Chris Hogg hails Northampton reaction against Rochdale Peeblesshire News
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Northampton boss Chris Hogg hailed the “outstanding reaction” of his players after they fought back from 2-1 down to beat Rochdale 3-2. Owen Dale gave the Cobblers an early lead at Sixfields but two goals in as many minutes from Ed Francis and Cian Hayes turned things around at the start of the second half. However, Elliott List levelled just after the hour-mark before Lee Evans won it from the penalty spot with 16 minutes to play. “It was a bit of a roller-coaster and it’s another experience for us as a team and as a group of people,” said Hogg. “We’ve already been through a lot of experiences this season, some good and some not so good, but I’m really pleased for the players today – I thought their reaction in the second half was outstanding. “The game should have been dead and buried for me in the first half. One goal was the very least we deserved and I spoke at half-time about being ruthless and then you blink and you’re 2-1 down and that’s a lesson for us. “You can’t wait to go 2-1 down to start playing again, but Listy came on and I thought he was terrific. “We changed the shape slightly and we wrestled the momentum back.

candidates.source_summary: Rochdale manager Ian Watson described the penalty that proved decisive in Saturday’s 3-2 defeat at Sixfields as ‘really harsh’.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Kane Taylor was adjudged to have had his arm in an unnatural position when blocking Elliott List’s cross with 16 minutes to play. Referee Callum Jones took his time before pointing to the spot and Lee Evans made no mistake from 12 yards to complete Northampton’s comeback after Dale had found themselves 2-1 in front. Earlier, the home side dominated the first half and would have been out of sight if not for Sam Waller. The Rochdale goalkeeper made a series of saves both before and after Owen Dale’s opener. “We didn’t start the game well at all," admitted Watson. “The opposition got on top of us and deservedly took the lead. We came more into it later in the first half and did have a couple of chances before half-time. “We demanded more energy and more intensity in the second half and we got that and we scored the two goals, but I felt we then dropped off too much and gave them too much space. “But the penalty is really harsh. He’s falling back, the ball hits his hand from a very short distance and the ref takes a long time to think about it. It’s a tough one. “But there’s no papering over any cracks. We weren’t good enough to win the game and that’s because we didn’t start the game well enough. Our goalkeeper has made a couple of great saves and I felt we had a real fear and anxiety about getting on the ball and that’s not the team we want to be. “We wanted to change the mentality and mindset at half-time and come out on the front foot and the boys did really well to get back into the game. They did everything they could and they worked hard as hard as they could - that’s not the reason we didn’t win the game.”

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Hundreds of knives, machetes, swords, axes and other blades have been surrendered as part of Greater Manchester Police’s ongoing operation against knife crime. As part of Operation Sceptre, there are three permanent knife surrender bins across the borough, outside police stations in Rochdale, Heywood and Middleton. The bins have been in place for two years and allow people to hand in deadly weapons anonymously. The latest collection on Thursday totalled 381 items surrendered, with 293 at Heywood, 47 in Middleton and 41 in Rochdale. Knuckle dusters and a blank-firing 8mm pistol and ammunition were also handed in. GMP shared: “The bins allow people to safely and anonymously surrender knives and other weapons. “Among the items surrendered was a blank-firing 8mm pistol and accompanying ammunition. While designed to fire blank cartridges, these weapons can still cause harm, cause significant alarm to members of the public, and can be difficult to distinguish from viable firearms. candidates.source_summary: 'Angelina' has told how she wants to move 200 miles away
candidates.source_body_excerpt: A victim of Rochdale grooming gang ringleader Shabir Ahmed has told how she fears he's now living near her - and how she's preparing to move more than 200 miles away as a result. Ahmed - known by his victims as 'Daddy' - was sentenced to 19 years in prison at Liverpool Crown Court in 2012 as one of nine men convicted of offences against five girls. He was released in July after serving 14 years. In a situation that has caused a diplomatic row, the 73-year-old can't be deported because of a 1971 law applying to Commonwealth citizens who arrived in the UK more than 50 years ago. It is being called a 'loophole'. Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter Ahmed has been stripped of his British citizenship, leaving him solely as a Pakistani national. Following his release, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said her intention was to change the legal loophole to make it possible to deport those convicted of serious crimes , including terrorism and child sexual exploitation. Pakistan has insisted it will not accept Ahmed's return. Ms Mahmood said the government was preparing to bring forward an ammendment to The Immigration and Asylum Bill because of the case of Ahmed. It went through its third reading in the House of Commons on Tuesday (November 17) and passed by 290 votes to 94. It will now progress to the House of Lords for scrutiny. Sky News interviewed 'Angelina' - not her real name - who told how she was raped by Ahmed as a teenager. She recalled going to a hospital after one attack, but said she was left with 'no support'. "They left me like I was an aninal in the world that you leave in a cage," she said. Ahmed, it is understood, is prevented from being in Rochdale and Greater Manchester as part of his release on licence arrangements. But Angelina said she fears he's been placed 'close' to where she lives. "That's the fear that I have," she said. She said she's now been accepted onto a list to relocate 200 miles away. "I have always got my eyes open at all times because I don't want him to bump into me," she said. The government, meanwhile, has refused to say whether it would impose sanctions on Pakistan to secure Ahmed's deportation.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Andrew Kowalczyk lived on the College Bank estate for 27 years but says he is now happy in his new home After 27 years living in the Seven Sisters tower blocks in Rochdale, Andrew Kowalczyk did not want to leave. But he said he felt the demolition of the flats, which have dominated the town's skyline since the 1960s, was "inevitable" and he was now relieved to have been rehoused. Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) announced last week that the blocks would be bulldozed and replaced with a new College Bank estate of about 600 homes. It comes after a 10-year campaign by residents who wanted the flats to be refurbished and not knocked down but RBH said the demolition was the only "realistic" option. Kowalczyk, 61, who lived in the Mardyke block, said he was reluctant to move out of his "secure" home and the "great views" but he has since been rehomed in a bungalow in Lower Falinge and was now "delighted with it". Residents started to move out of the flats in October last year after long-term safety concerns were raised in October last year. The blocks are almost all empty, with 78 homes out of 766 currently occupied.

The new facility which opened this month has IT labs and an immersive virtual reality suite based at the landmark Reid building, part of Hopwood Hall College’s Middleton campus. As finishing touches are still being made to the exterior and landscaping, Cllr Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and co-operation at Rochdale Council was given a preview this week, during a visit arranged to thank the college for its support of Rochdale Feel Good Festival. Hopwood Hall College was one of the main sponsors of this summer’s festival, an event it has supported since 2019, even hosting the main stage at the Rochdale campus in 2022 while the town hall closed for refurbishment. Julia Heap, principal and CEO of Hopwood Hall College, showed Cllr Smith around the site, including a stop at the historic chapel which has been transformed into an innovative skills hub with classrooms, computer labs and a virtual reality suite providing T-Level courses in engineering and manufacturing. Julia Heap, Hopwood Hall College principal and CEO (right) is thanked by Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and co-operation at Rochdale Borough Council. Mrs Heap described it as possibly the most unique learning environment in the UK. She said: “This iconic building has always been a favourite with students, staff and college visitors, but now it has a completely new lease of life as a beacon for technical education and skills training while maintaining its character and heritage.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Repair cafes, new hubs for families to buy affordable school uniforms and workshops in upcycling and restoration have all been funded by a scheme to reduce waste and save people money in Greater Manchester. Heywood Uniform Hub CIC is among 19 community groups to receive a total of £200,000 from the Renew Community Fund, supporting community-led projects to keep household items in use for longer, ease pressure on household budgets and bring people together. The increased cost-of-living can make it harder for families to afford everyday essentials such as furniture, electronics, toys and uniforms. At the same time, useful items are often thrown away rather than being passed on or fixed, as the skills needed to mend them have been lost. Now in its sixth year, the Renew Community Fund has awarded a total of £1.3 million to 128 local, community-led projects that help these issues across Greater Manchester. Renew is a joint collaboration between Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) and waste and resources company SUEZ. Money is raised via sales of preloved items that have been donated by Greater Manchester residents at recycling centres. Renew Greater Manchester repairs, refurbishes or upcycles and sells them, with money raised reinvested back into local communities. This year saw a record-breaking number of applications, with a total of 149 projects bidding for funding. READ MORE: New trial will ‘get tough’ with prolific shoplifters

candidates.source_summary: Rochdale manager Ian Watson has identified areas that he feels his side can exploit when they face Northampton at Sixfields on Saturday.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Both teams go into the game keen for three points to kick-start their respective seasons. Cobblers are 19th in League Two on 15 points, above 22nd-placed Dale on goal difference. “Northampton are coming off the back of a really good result at Salford,” said Watson, who replaced the Stockport-bound Jimmy McNulty in the summer. “I’ve watched that game a couple of times and I thought they played really well. He added: “We’re really confident we can build on our performance against York. Training has been very competitive and everyone is pushing each other. “We need to get better and we need to be more consistent but my belief in this group and in myself has not wavered at all. candidates.source_summary: Springhill Hospice in Rochdale has won three awards through the Royal Horticultural Society’s In Bloom programme, including Best Hospice Garden in the North West for 2026.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Springhill Hospice in Rochdale has won three awards through the Royal Horticultural Society’s In Bloom programme, including Best Hospice Garden in the North West for 2026. The hospice received Level 5 Outstanding, the highest rating in the Rochdale in Bloom It’s Your Neighbourhood Awards. It also received a Level 5 Outstanding Five Year Achievement Award for maintaining that standard over the five years it has entered. Springhill was named Best Hospice Garden in the North West 2026 at the North West in Bloom Awards. The regional award recognises the role hospice gardens play in providing welcoming spaces for patients, families, visitors and staff. A team of 18 volunteer gardeners maintains the grounds throughout the year. Patients and their loved ones use the gardens to sit together, spend time in quiet surroundings and enjoy the changing seasons. The grounds are also used by visitors, volunteers and staff. Claire Connely, head gardener at Springhill Hospice, said, “I couldn’t be prouder of everyone, but especially our magnificent garden team and all the marvellous things they have achieved together. “Week after week, come rain or shine, our volunteers give their time, skills and energy to care for the gardens and create something truly special for everyone who visits Springhill. “To receive three awards, and particularly to be named Best Hospice Garden in the North West, is wonderful recognition of everything they put into making our gardens what they are. They are an astonishingly beautiful and important part of Springhill, and these awards belong to every person who has played a part in creating and caring for them.” The hospice’s Business Buddies and corporate volunteers regularly contribute their time, expertise and practical help. Local people and organisations donate plant pots, coffee grounds, plants and gardening materials. The team at 3 Pitts allotment grows and donates 400 begonias each spring, which are planted throughout the hospice grounds.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Rochdale Masters Rugby League and Mayfield Movers have raised £14,698.67 for charities and community rugby league through two walking challenges. Their latest walk raised £6,141.80, with three charities set to receive at least £1,500 each. Walkers set off from Ince Rose Bridge ARLFC in Wigan at 6.30am on Saturday 31 October 2026 for the 44-mile All Together Walk. The route took in 10 community rugby league clubs across Greater Manchester, passing through Leigh, Salford and Bury before the group reached Rochdale Mayfield ARLFC at 9.48pm. Volunteers and supporters helped the group during the walk, which took more than 15 hours. Rugby league clubs along the route welcomed the walkers with refreshments and encouragement. The Motor Neurone Disease Association, the Rugby League Cares Brain Health Fund and Springhill Hospice in Rochdale will each receive at least £1,500. The three charities are due to receive a combined minimum of £4,500. Rochdale Masters has committed to covering all fundraising transaction fees so that each charity receives its full allocation. The remaining proceeds will go towards developing the Rochdale Masters section and helping people stay active, socially connected and involved in rugby league. The same groups raised £8,556.87 in October 2025 by walking 52 miles from Rochdale to Blackpool. Mayfield Movers is a community walking group based at Rochdale Mayfield ARLFC, where Rochdale Masters also operates. Both groups aim to help people of different ages, backgrounds and abilities take part in physical activity, build friendships and improve their physical and mental wellbeing.

Thiago tragically died after being rushed to hospital from the Cosy Toes nursery on Mainway East. Emergency crews were called to the nursery on November 2. Pictures from the scene showed a large response with three police vehicles, an ambulance and rapid response paramedic car in attendance. The air ambulance was also pictured landing nearby. Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter Sadly, Thiago died in hospital on November 5. His family are being supported by specialist officers. An inquest opening has been scheduled at Rochdale Coroners' Court for November 25. The Cosy Toes nursery has been closed following his death. Greater Manchester Police confirmed an investigation has been launched. Representatives for the nursery described Thiago as a 'wonderful and beautiful child'. A spokesperson for the nursery said: "We are all heartbroken to hear of the tragic news of the child’s passing. "He was a wonderful and beautiful child, and our thoughts and prayers are all with his family at this terrible time. We will of course give our fullest possible assistance in every way possible to the enquiries that must rightly follow this tragic event." Ofsted has suspended the nursery's registration in the wake of the incident, meaning the nursery will be closed for six weeks whilst enquiries are carried out. An Ofsted spokesperson said: "Our thoughts are with the family of the young boy and everyone affected by this deeply distressing incident. "We have worked closely with the police, and we have suspended the nursery's registration. We will continue to support the police and other agencies in their enquiries. We are unable to comment further while the police investigation is ongoing." A GMP spokesperson said no arrests have been made at this stage. "As the circumstances leading up to the boy’s death occurred in a care setting, and in line with usual procedure, a police investigation has been opened", the force spokesperson added. Detective Chief Inspector Claire Brennan said: "This is an incredibly tragic development in a deeply upsetting incident and our thoughts remain with the boy's family. candidates.source_summary: Rochdale man jailed for life after murdering wife and hiding her body under the bed for two days The Manc
candidates.source_body_excerpt: He only reported the incident once the body began to smell. A man from Rochdale has been sentenced to life in prison after murdering his wife and hiding her body under the bed for two days. Having previously denied the offence, Kyle Howard appeared at Manchester Crown Court this week where he finally pleaded guilty to, and was then subsequently sentenced to life for, the murder of 44-year-old Keeley Aspinall. His sentencing comes after officers from Greater Manchester Police (GMP) responded to a report made by Howard at around 4pm on 25 May 2026, who stated that he had killed his wife in their home on Tweedale Street in Rochdale – adding that he had stabbed her to two days earlier, and was only now reporting the incident because her body was beginning to smell. When police arrived at the address, they discovered Keeley’s body concealed underneath a bed, and Howard was immediately arrested on suspicion of murder. Paramedics attended the scene along with police , but Howard was reported as telling them: “There is no point being here, I’ve done it, she’s dead, she’s been dead for two days.” After his arrest, Howard made several confessions whilst being booked into police custody – including making comments such as: “It’s her own f*cking fault”, “I’m not denying it”, and “I’ll admit it, I’m not bothered.” When questioned on the incident, Howard stated that the pair had been drinking and began to argue in the kitchen.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Greater Manchester mayor Bev Craig has said a social landlord is running housing stock in Rochdale ‘into the ground’ following the announcement the Seven Sisters tower blocks are to be bulldozed. On Monday (November 16), Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) said it intended to demolish the 766 flats and replace them with a mix of 601 new flats and town houses. The decision brings to an end an era of uncertainty for the site, officially called College Bank. The towers were first earmarked for demolition a decade ago. Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter Speaking on BBC Radio Manchester’s weekly mayoral phone in show, Ms Craig said ‘knocking down stock without a clear plan’ as to when homes would be replaced was ‘incredibly disappointing’. She added that ‘there’s a long-standing issue with the provider’ and the matter had ‘been 10 years in the making’. Around 80 households remain at Seven Sisters with the previous uncertainty leading to many tenants departing. Campaigners have fought to stop demolition ever since it was first mooted in 2016. They want to see the 1960s block refurbished instead. It comes as RBH bosses released computer-generated images showing how the site could look once the towers have been knocked down and the plot redeveloped. Ms Craig was answering the concerns from a campaigner called Mark. He said that since 2012, social housing stock Rochdale had been depleted from 13,700 units and ‘if we lose College Bank and Lower Falinge, that figure will be down to 11,000’. Ms Craig was told at a campaign meeting for residents on Wednesday evening (November 18), ‘the anger was palpable’ and that it was ‘scandalous’ that 20,000 people were on the social housing waiting list in the borough. The mayor said: “To get to a situation where a social housing provider is essentially running stock into the ground is not acceptable. I’m trying to bring together Rochdale Boroughwide Housing with the council to get them to listen to the voice of community. “I’m disappointed that this is where we’ve come to. In the middle of a housing crisis, knocking down stock without a clear plan as to when RBH is going to be able to replace those social homes that we desperately need is incredibly disappointing. “I received the notification from RBH that the decision had been made and that it was going ahead. That’s a little bit at odds from the last meeting that we had with them. “I can understand residents’ frustration on this. This has been a long fight, and I know there’s a lot of anger out there. I think there’s a long-standing issue with the provider that we’re talking about here.” RBH says it would be too expensive and would take too long to refurbish the blocks, so has opted to redevelop the site. Bosses estimate it would take 12 years to refurbish and cost £269m – around £388,000 per flat. The decision was made by RBH after more than a year of working with the ‘College Bank Task Force’, which includes the council and Greater Manchester Combined Authority. RBH said that included ‘a detailed review of all available scenarios’. Ms Craig said she would make clear to RBH that she ‘want[s] to know a clear plan’. candidates.source_body_excerpt: Hundreds of families are currently living in temporary accommodation in Rochdale . And it comes at a huge cost to the council. Now the town hall has a £5.6m plan to make sure temporary accommodation is suitable and more cost-effective over the next four years. The local authority has devised a framework that would help them control the types of housing they offer those at risk of homelessness, who can be some of the most vulnerable in society. As of the beginning of November, there are 387 Rochdale households in temporary accommodation, according to council papers. Of these, 250 of are families with children and there 13 families in Bed & Breakfasts and five families in out of borough placements. Use of hotels and B&Bs is the most expensive provision and is also more likely not to be up to standard, a report found. A higher complexity of need for those using the council’s housing service as well as a decrease in social housing supply in the borough is what has sparked the town hall to take action. The new framework would allow the town hall to have greater oversight and influence over the local supported accommodation. This plan would see the types of accommodation into four ‘Lots’ and is estimated to cost £5.6m over four years. Lot 1 and Lot 2 would incur the largest expense at an estimated £4.9m, because they include B&Bs and nightly paid accommodation for the homeless.

candidates.source_summary: The number of people claiming unemployment-related benefits in Rochdale rose by 215 to 8,825 in October 2026, from 8,610 in September 2026. That is 6.1% of residents aged 16 to 64, compared with 5.9% the month before. A year earlier, in October 2025, the figure was 8,565. The claimant count is published by the Office for National Statistics through Nomis; the latest month is provisional and can be revised.
